query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An aging heat‐treatment that promotes the precipitation of a coherent gamma prime (Ni3Al) phase in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature yield strength compared to the same alloy without aging.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized single-phase high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents (e.g., nearly equiatomic Ti and Ni) along with three other elements (each between 5–35 at%) produced by arc melting and solution treatment, with a small aluminum content added (approximately 5–15 at%) to enable gamma prime precipitation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a post-casting aging treatment by heating the alloy at an optimized temperature (e.g., ≈800°C) for a set duration (e.g., 4 hours) in an inert or vacuum atmosphere so as to induce the precipitation of nano-scale gamma prime particles.
generation.conditions: After casting and solution treatment, subject a sample of the alloy to aging at about 800°C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere, then air-cool. Evaluate mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and creep resistance) at elevated temperatures (target range of 800°C to 1200°C) under controlled strain rate conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a homogeneously dispersed, coherent nano-scale gamma prime (Ni3Al) precipitate phase within the high-entropy single-phase matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the gamma prime precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing the yield strength and creep resistance of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The gamma prime precipitation is expected to increase the elevated-temperature yield strength (by roughly 20–30% compared to the unaged, homogeneous alloy) and improve creep resistance within the operating temperature window.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in its solution-treated (single-phase) state without an aging treatment.
generation.boundary: Applicable to alloys satisfying the HEA composition definition (each of at least five elements present at 5–35 at%), operating at elevated temperatures up to about 1200°C, and containing a modest aluminum content (approximately 5–15 at%) to promote gamma prime formation without compromising the multi-principal-element balance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength enhancement and precipitate stability at ultra-high temperatures depends on the fine-tuning of the alloy composition and aging parameters; experimental calibration is required to confirm the optimum processing window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare the target Ti-Ni-primary high-entropy alloy with an added 5–15 at% Al to enable gamma prime precipitation. Divide the alloy into two batches: one batch remains in the as-solution-treated (single-phase) condition while the second batch is aged at 800°C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere. Subject both batches to mechanical testing (tensile and/or creep tests) at elevated temperatures in the range of 800°C – 1200°C. Concurrently, characterize the microstructures of both batches using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect the presence and distribution of gamma prime precipitates.
measurements: Creep rate or strain vs. time under load at high temperature
TEM images showing nano-scale gamma prime precipitate size/distribution
Phase analysis via XRD to confirm precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., less than 10% improvement) in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the solution-treated alloy, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of the intended nano-scale gamma prime precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,].
